narrative: The writeup says the rotating-picture format made year depth much more important than expected and turned the author's original 1990 pick into an obvious mistake. Most of the commentary then celebrates the unusually deep lineup and personal memories attached to 2000.
headline: The picture format reveals 2000's superior depth

narrative: 1996 is portrayed as a thin year carried by a few excellent games, while 1989 is described as even weaker outside Mega Man 2. The writeup is especially personal, using Mario RPG and Diablo as anchors for memories tied to the year.
headline: 1996 advances behind a few heavyweight classics

narrative: The writeup finds the scale of 1991's win surprising because much of its lineup looks mid-tier outside Super Mario World. It treats 1988 as an awkward year of sequels and experiments that was far weaker than the Zelda name alone might imply.
headline: 1991 crushes a surprisingly weak 1988

narrative: The writeup is mostly an extended anti-Warcraft 3 and anti-2002 rant, with only a brief argument that 2010 had the better overall lineup.
headline: The match becomes an anti-Warcraft 3 rant

narrative: The writeup calls this the first match where casual brackets were badly burned, with 2004 inflated by World of Warcraft and other mainstream names. It treats 1994 as vastly deeper and more aligned with GameFAQs tastes.
headline: 1994 punishes casual faith in 2004

narrative: A debated matchup stayed competitive early before 2011 took control and pulled away. The writeup argues that 2011 was simply the deeper and better year despite 2006's Zelda and Kingdom Hearts headliners.
headline: 2011 wins the first genuinely competitive year matchup

narrative: 1998 is presented as the overwhelming contest favorite and treated as championship caliber from its first appearance. The writeup deliberately saves most of its 1998 retrospective for the final while giving 1993 credit for several beloved cult games.
headline: 1998 opens like the obvious contest favorite

narrative: The writeup uses 2016 as an example of why rally potential depends heavily on bracket placement, arguing that no outside push could realistically save it here. It then frames 1992's lineup, led by A Link to the Past and Sonic 2, as overwhelming.
headline: 1992 kills the feared 2016 rally before it can start

narrative: A heavily debated year matchup became straightforward once 2003 established control. The writeup says a mainline console Zelda title gave 2003 the decisive edge over 2013's strong but less imposing lineup.
headline: 2003 settles a heavily debated year matchup

narrative: The feared Undertale rally never mattered because 2015 was immediately placed against a year the writeup considered much stronger. The result closes an opening round the author regards as one of the least entertaining in contest history.
headline: 2005 ends 2015's rally hopes and a miserable round

narrative: 1995 advanced but looked far too weak for the overall top seed, stalling for hours against 1987 before finally separating. The writeup treats this as the point where its anticipated showdown with 2001 stopped looking competitive.
headline: 1995 advances with a major warning sign

narrative: 2001 crushed a 2008 lineup the writeup considered legitimately solid, reinforcing how extreme the contest's round-to-round blowouts had become. The result also made the coming 2001-versus-1995 matchup look heavily tilted toward 2001.
headline: 2001 keeps Blowout City rolling

narrative: 1997's rout looked like a championship-quality performance at the time and seemed to set up a serious challenge to 1998. In hindsight, the writeup treats the result more as evidence that 2007 was unusually weak.
headline: 1997 looks like a title contender against 2007

anomaly_note: The writeup says 2000 was effectively denied a fair chance because Pokémon GSC was omitted from its match picture while 1996 received an unusually strong set of representative games. It explicitly argues that the picture imbalance likely decided the match.
narrative: The match stayed close overnight before 1996 pulled away once the morning vote arrived. The writeup considers the final result tainted by a picture policy that failed to represent 2000's strongest possible lineup.
headline: Picture selection costs 2000 a fair fight

narrative: 1991's weak performance against 2002 immediately damaged the author's upset hopes for its next match. The writeup argues that the contest's year format had made normal transitive strength comparisons almost useless.
headline: 1991 survives but loses its upset case

narrative: 1994 comfortably beat 2011 and looked substantially stronger than 1991 had in the neighboring matchup. The writeup treats the result as confirmation that their next-round debate was already effectively settled.
headline: 1994 makes the 1991 debate look one-sided

narrative: 1998 demolished a year centered on A Link to the Past and produced what the writeup calls the best performance of the round. The result is treated as conclusive evidence that only a major rally could stop 1998 from winning the contest.
headline: 1998 demolishes 1992 and seizes the championship

narrative: 2003 handled a matchup some had worried about and advanced without serious danger. The writeup mostly uses the result to emphasize how hopeless 2003 looked against 1998 in the next round.
headline: 2003 advances directly into the 1998 buzzsaw

narrative: 1995 briefly made its matchup with 2001 look like a classic before 2001 began pulling away and never looked back. The writeup explicitly calls it a fair fight and rejects picture excuses for the result.
headline: 2001 wins a fair fight against fading 1995

narrative: 1997 crushed 1996 and appeared almost as dominant as 1998, making a 1997-versus-1998 final feel inevitable. The writeup stresses how impressive such a blowout looked this deep in the bracket.
headline: 1997 keeps looking like a finalist

anomaly_note: The writeup argues that excluding console launches from every match picture unfairly hurt 1991 in particular because the Super Nintendo was one of its strongest assets. It says 1994 may still have won, but the picture policy made the matchup fundamentally unfair.
narrative: 1991 won the opening board vote and then was steadily run over by 1994. The writeup's main story is anger that system releases were omitted from a contest supposedly about entire gaming years.
headline: Missing console pictures taint 1994's win over 1991

anomaly_note: The writeup explicitly likens 1998's rout of 2003 to a Zelda SFF beating, with Ocarina of Time effectively suppressing a Wind Waker-centered year.
narrative: 1998 produced another enormous late-round blowout and made 2003 look completely outclassed. The writeup treats the result as the year-contest equivalent of a dominant same-fanbase Zelda matchup.
headline: 1998 SFFs 2003 into the ground

narrative: 2001 pulled off what the writeup considers one of the most inexplicable non-rally upsets in contest history. After a long early struggle, 2001 controlled both the overnight and daytime portions and never allowed 1997 a real comeback.
headline: 2001 shocks 1997 in an inexplicable semifinal upset

narrative: 1998 comfortably eliminated 1994 in a semifinal that was notable mainly for how predictable the contest had become. The writeup uses the result to compare late-round blowout records rather than to describe any real competitive drama.
headline: 1998 cruises through a predictable semifinal

narrative: 1998 ended the contest with a historically dominant championship performance and completed the run the writeup had expected from the start. The analysis turns into a long celebration of the year's unusually deep lineup and of many beloved games finally being attached to a contest winner.
headline: 1998 closes the contest with a historic championship rout

narrative: Dante won the opening matchup comfortably but failed to look as overwhelming as the writeup expected from the contest's top overall seed. Cuphead's respectable showing is treated as evidence that the indie newcomer was underseeded rather than truly dangerous.
headline: Dante opens comfortably but looks weak for the top seed

narrative: Lightning turned a match that had generated second-match paranoia into an immediate blowout. The writeup treats Chloe as likely bottom-tier fodder and says the result did little to prove Lightning had genuinely recovered.
headline: Lightning crushes Chloe and ends the second-match paranoia

narrative: Chun-Li beat Spyro in a debated matchup, but Spyro stayed competitive enough to validate his recent nostalgia-driven recovery. The writeup explicitly rejects the old Jug Factor as the reason for the result.
headline: Chun-Li survives Spyro without any Jug Factor

narrative: Ganondorf crushed Neku far more severely than expected and immediately looked like the division favorite. The writeup treats the result as an early sign that Zelda, Switch and Smash hype would dominate the contest.
headline: Ganondorf opens with a huge Zelda-era statement

narrative: Vivi handled Yu Narukami in a routine blowout and stood out as one of the few Final Fantasy characters still retaining old strength. The writeup mentions possible Square overlap only as an uncertainty rather than a confirmed explanation.
headline: Vivi stays strong while Square collapses around him

narrative: Aya Brea turned a heavily debated matchup into a stable, comfortable win over Victor Sullivan. The writeup treats the result as another example of 1990s GameFAQs nostalgia beating a newer Western series.
headline: Aya Brea crushes the Victor Sullivan debate

narrative: Donkey Kong demolished Tidus in a matchup built around two characters with long reputations for choking. The writeup attributes the result to Donkey Kong's renewed relevance, broader Nintendo momentum and Tidus's continued decline.
headline: Donkey Kong wins the battle of legendary chokers

narrative: Leon comfortably beat Dragonborn and looked strong enough to justify confidence in a deep run. Dragonborn's large recovery over the day is treated as a trend quirk rather than a meaningful threat.
headline: Leon opens strongly against Dragonborn

narrative: Zero handled Primrose in a routine top-seed matchup, though the writeup gives Primrose credit for avoiding a complete collapse. Any possible benefit from the simultaneous Monika rally is described as unclear.
headline: Zero wins while Primrose earns a little respect

anomaly_note: The writeup says the simultaneous Monika rally brought in outside voters who disproportionately favored Knuckles, with one analysis explicitly saying Square was hurt by the spillover.
narrative: Knuckles crushed a matchup many experts had favored Zidane to win and extended his remarkable history of first-round success. Rally spillover from the neighboring Monika poll is treated as an extra tailwind, not the sole reason for the upset.
headline: Knuckles beats Zidane with help from rally spillover

narrative: Master Hand crushed Noctis in a matchup that had been treated as a true tossup beforehand. The writeup sees the result as one of the clearest signs that modern Final Fantasy had fallen badly while Smash-era Nintendo strength had risen.
headline: Master Hand humiliates Noctis in a debated matchup

anomaly_note: The writeup explicitly says Monika received a real Reddit and community rally, visible in the higher turnout and several stalls or small cuts, but that the push was far too weak to threaten Wario.
narrative: Monika drew the outside support many bracketmakers feared, but Wario remained safely in control throughout. The writeup treats the failed upset as evidence that small fandom rallies were much less dangerous under the contest's anti-rally setup.
headline: Monika rallies but never seriously threatens Wario

narrative: Yoshi delivered the expected blowout over Shantae, but the match sparked a disproportionate argument over whether Shantae had any meaningful contest strength. The writeup ultimately treats her as ordinary fodder with a dedicated niche fanbase.
headline: Yoshi crushes Shantae and starts a fodder argument

narrative: Velvet turned a mildly debated matchup with James Sunderland into an easy win and gave the Tales series a rare character-contest victory. The writeup mentions recognizability and presentation as possible helpers but still treats the result as fundamentally legitimate.
headline: Velvet gives Tales a rare clean character win

narrative: Pikachu overwhelmed a stable measuring-stick opponent in Scorpion and immediately looked near-elite. The writeup treats the result as the first major evidence that Pokémon, and Pikachu specifically, would be a serious force in the contest.
headline: Pikachu announces himself as a near-elite threat

anomaly_note: The writeup explicitly calls Kratos's unusually large win over John Marston SFF, arguing that two similar Western tough-guy fanbases overlapped heavily and that the stronger, more established Kratos suppressed Marston.
narrative: Kratos produced by far one of the strongest performances of his contest career while Marston looked far weaker than his game-level popularity suggested. The writeup attributes much of the gap to same-audience suppression.
headline: Kratos SFFs John Marston in a huge statement

narrative: Sora won easily but failed the writeup's real test: looking strong enough for a top seed before the coming Red matchup. Ryo's modest resistance immediately became another warning sign for Sora's familiar pattern of high seeding and underachievement.
headline: Sora wins but immediately looks vulnerable

narrative: Pokémon Trainer Red crushed an unusually high-seeded newcomer and looked stronger than Sora had in the neighboring top-seed matchup. The result made their impending Round Two contest feel like a genuine tossup.
headline: Red crushes Neptune and puts Sora on notice

narrative: Crash decisively beat Cecil in another matchup the Final Fantasy IV protagonist had been widely expected to win. The writeup treats the result as both a Crash nostalgia boost and the formal birth of the Cecil Harvey Never Wins meme.
headline: Crash turns Cecil Harvey Never Wins into canon

narrative: Big Boss beat a Smash-boosted Ridley comfortably, though Ridley performed well enough to show clear improvement. The writeup frames the result as a rare case where an established non-Nintendo character resisted the contest's Nintendo surge.
headline: Big Boss withstands Ridley's Smash boost

narrative: Alucard beat Peach without much drama in a matchup that some had overhyped because of Nintendo momentum. The writeup sees both characters as having looked respectable and rejects any need for a firm SFF explanation.
headline: Alucard calmly handles the Peach upset hype

narrative: Yuna overwhelmed the Board 8-favorite Godot in a matchup that was never competitive after the opening moments. The writeup treats Godot's appearance as a community victory even though the broader site gave him little support.
headline: Yuna crushes a beloved Board 8 newcomer

narrative: Kefka turned one of Round One's hardest prediction calls into a comfortable win over former champion L-Block. The writeup treats the result as another example of Kefka's unpredictability and of fading support for rallybait joke characters.
headline: Kefka routs L-Block in a classic prediction trap

narrative: Bomberman demolished the heavily overseeded Kiryu and produced one of the bracket's clearest seeding embarrassments. The writeup treats the result as evidence that recognizability still mattered more than recent niche popularity.
headline: Bomberman embarrasses an overseeded Kiryu

narrative: 2B crushed Cayde-6 and immediately proved she had legitimate contest strength even if her top seeding was inflated. Cayde is treated as one of the weakest entrants in the entire field.
headline: 2B validates herself against bottom-tier Cayde
